 18 November 2026 - Advertisement - Indonesia is calling for stronger sustainable peatland governance through data harmonisation, management based on Peatland Hydrological Units (PHUs), and regional cooperation to prevent peatland fires and transboundary haze across Southeast Asia and the Western Pacific.
 Dr. Agus Justianto, Chair of the Interim Secretariat of the International Tropical Peatlands Center (ITPC), emphasised that peatland management must be grounded in accurate and reliable data to support policymaking, restoration planning, and stronger international cooperation.

 “Indonesia has 24.6 million hectares of Peatland Hydrological Units, based on peatland hydrological mapping. Having a common data reference is essential to ensure that management planning, restoration targets, and measurement, reporting, and verification systems are built on a consistent foundation,” Agus said.
 Agus made the remarks during a dialogue titled “Building Coordination for Multi-stakeholder Collaboration on Sustainable Management in Indonesia, Malaysia and Papua New Guinea,” organised under the Western Pacific Sustainable Peatland Management (SAGU) Project at the ASEAN Pavilion during the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, on Tuesday (17 November).
 Dr. Bambang Supriyanto, Vice-Chair of the ITPC Interim Secretariat, explained that differences in data on peatland ecosystem coverage and forest and land fires must be assessed in light of the methodologies, geographical scope, and reporting periods used.
 “Responsibility for addressing peatland fires and transboundary haze cannot rest with a single country. Shared responsibility is needed through partnerships between governments and businesses, consistent law enforcement, and stronger regional coordination to ensure effective fire prevention,” Bambang said.
 Bambang also highlighted the importance of accountability in investment and operational activities related to peatland management, including cross-border investments.
 According to Bambang, public-private partnerships must be supported by transparency, oversight, and law enforcement to ensure that peatland management does not create environmental risks affecting neighbouring countries.
 Meanwhile, Dr. Vong Sok, Head of the Environment Division and Assistant Director of the Sustainable Development Directorate at the ASEAN Secretariat, stressed the importance of strengthening regional cooperation on sustainable peatland management and transboundary haze, which affects the environment, public health, and economies across ASEAN member states.
 He noted that peatland fires require a collective approach involving data harmonisation, stronger early warning systems, and coordinated policies and preventive measures among countries.
 “Addressing transboundary haze requires shared commitment and responsibility among ASEAN member states through the exchange of accurate information, stronger cross-border cooperation, and coordinated peatland fire prevention measures to protect the region’s environment and communities,” Vong Sok said.
 Swetha Peteru, Senior Scientist and Principal Investigator of the Western Pacific Sustainable Peatland Management (SAGU) Project, highlighted the importance of collaboration among Indonesia, Malaysia, and Papua New Guinea in advancing sustainable peatland management based on science, landscape approaches, and community participation.
 She emphasised that knowledge exchange, capacity building, financing, and monitoring are essential to maintaining peatlands’ ecological functions while improving community well-being.
 “Through the SAGU Project, we are promoting cross-border cooperation that integrates peatland conservation, restoration, and responsible use to support local economies and the achievement of regional climate targets,” Swetha said.
 The forum also explored opportunities to strengthen policies, climate finance, knowledge exchange, and capacity building in measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) systems, climate vulnerability assessments, and the implementation of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs).
 Cooperation between Indonesia and Malaysia, as ASEAN member states, and Papua New Guinea, as an ASEAN observer, was considered important in strengthening the region’s collective contribution to implementing the Paris Agreement.

 Looking ahead, regional collaboration through the SAGU Project and ITPC is expected to accelerate the adoption of landscape-based peatland management, data harmonisation, fire prevention, and community economic development aligned with the ecological functions of peatlands.
 For Indonesia, these efforts form a strategic part of supporting the FOLU Net Sink 2030 target, strengthening climate resilience, and ensuring that peatland ecosystem protection delivers lasting benefits for the environment, communities, and the regional economy.
